10.1109/SoutheastCon63549.2026.11476704: Kinetic facades can improve building performance by regulating daylight and incident solar gains through controllable geometry. In practice, many facade prototypes remain isolated subsystems with limited sensing, limited coordination with lighting and HVAC, and control policies that do not transfer across seasons and occupancy patterns. This paper presents an Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) and digital twin framework that couples multi-sensor monitoring, edge autonomy, and cloud analytics to support repeatable deployment. A functional taxonomy is introduced to map facade intent to measurable objectives and to make sensor selection and evaluation metrics explicit. Building on this foundation, we propose an occupancy-aware, multi-objective controller for louver-based facades that prioritizes visual comfort when spaces are occupied and shifts toward solar heat mitigation and operational efficiency when spaces are unoccupied. The control design integrates a digital-twinseeded surrogate model for fast prediction and includes online calibration to reduce sensitivity to site-specific effects such as sensor placement and interior reflectance. A deployment-oriented algorithm is provided with safety constraints, manual override, and telemetry for continuous improvement. The framework is demonstrated using a louver prototype and a digital twin irradiation analysis. The prototype exhibits actuation response on the order of seconds and illuminance regulation near a 300 lux target during occupied operation.
10.1109/SEFET65155.2025.11255452: Dynamic Partial Shading Conditions (DPSC) significantly impact the energy output of solar photovoltaic systems, leading to multiple local maxima in the power-voltage (P-V) curve and reducing energy efficiency. To resolve this challenge, advanced Maximum Power Point Tracking techniques have been developed to ensure optimal power extraction. This review focuses on three cutting-edge MPPT —Incremental Conductance with Differential Optimization (INC-DFO), Sovereign Butterfly Optimization (SBO), and Whale Optimization with Differential Evolution (WODE)—which have shown promising results in handling rapid shading transitions. These techniques are evaluated based on key performance parameters, including tracking speed, accuracy, adaptability to shading patterns, robustness, computational complexity, and convergence behavior. The analysis highlights that while INC-DFO offers moderate tracking speed and reliability, SBO provides the fastest and most robust convergence. WODE achieves a balance between precision and computational efficiency, making it an ideal choice for real-time applications. This review serves as a critical resource for researchers and engineers seeking efficient MPPT strategies to enhance PV system performance under dynamic shading scenarios.
10.1109/ICEPE65965.2025.11139553: Building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) systems play a crucial role in sustainable energy generation, especially when integrated into Virtual Power Plants (VPPs). However, dynamic shading conditions significantly impact the power output of BIPV systems, necessitating efficient Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) strategies. This study proposes an Adaptive MPPT Strategy for BIPV Systems Using MBGO Assisted P&O Under Dynamic Shading, combining the Perturb and Observe (P&O) technique assisted by Multiplayer Battle Game-Inspired Optimizer (MBGO) algorithm to enhance tracking efficiency and stability under fluctuating solar irradiance. The research presents a comparative study between tie-line connected and non-tie-line connected PV systems to evaluate their performance as Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) within a VPP framework. The proposed MPPT approach is designed to optimize power extraction while mitigating the effects of partial shading. The study conducts a detailed analysis under four different operating conditions for both tie-line and non-tie-line configurations, assessing power output improvements achieved through the proposed technique. Simulation results demonstrate that the MBGO-assisted P&O strategy significantly enhances power extraction efficiency, reducing oscillations and convergence time compared to conventional MPPT techniques. The findings indicate that tieline connected BIPV systems exhibit more stable energy contributions to the VPP, while non-tie-line systems benefit from improved standalone efficiency with the adaptive MPPT approach. The proposed methodology offers a robust solution for improving energy utilization in BIPV systems, ensuring reliable integration into smart grids and VPP networks.
10.1109/GIEST66547.2025.11387715: Photovoltaic (PV) systems are increasingly being deployed as a clean and sustainable energy source, but their efficiency is significantly impacted by environmental factors, particularly under partial shading conditions (PSC). These conditions introduce multiple local maxima in the power-voltage (P−V) curve, making it challenging for conventional maximum power point tracking (MPPT) techniques such as Perturb and Observe (P&O) to reliably track the global maximum power point (GMPP). This paper proposes a supervised machine learning (ML)-based MPPT strategy using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) regressor to directly predict the optimal duty cycle of a boost converter, leveraging inputs such as irradiance, temperature, and shading variation. A dynamic simulation environment is developed to evaluate and compare the proposed ML-based controller against the conventional P&O method. The model demonstrates improved tracking performance, especially under dynamic and partially shaded conditions. Quantitative performance metrics, including predicted maximum power point (MPP) accuracy, duty cycle optimization, and overall tracking efficiency, confirm the superiority of the ML-based approach for real-time MPPT applications.
10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3551226: In Mediterranean regions, traditional courtyard designs are celebrated for their passive cooling potential, yet modern mosques often rely heavily on energy-intensive cooling systems due to underperforming architectural strategies. This study addresses this paradox by leveraging parametric modeling to optimize courtyard-driven energy efficiency in the King Hussein Mosque, Jordan. Using a novel Grasshopper-based workflow integrating Ladybug, Honeybee, and Butterfly plugins, we quantify how courtyard orientation, enclosure, and fenestration impact Energy Use Intensity (EUI) and thermal comfort. Simulations revealed a baseline EUI of 111.132 kWh/m2 (EPC Rating E), with cooling demands contributing 20.432 kWh/m2 despite three courtyards designed for natural ventilation. Parametric testing of interventions—including partial courtyard enclosures and optimized window-to-wall ratios—reduced EUI to 98.989 kWh/m2 (EPC Rating D), achieving an 11% energy savings while maintaining the mosque's architectural integrity. Thermal comfort in the prayer hall improved by 15%, with UTCI thresholds shifting from "high heat stress" to "moderate comfort" during summer occupancy. This work pioneers the application of Grasshopper in mosque energy optimization, demonstrating its superiority over static simulation tools by enabling real-time, multi-variable adjustments tailored to intermittent prayer schedules. The findings challenge assumptions about courtyard efficacy in contemporary religious architecture, offering actionable retrofitting guidelines for designers: strategic partial enclosures, localized shading, and adaptive fenestration. By bridging computational design with cultural heritage preservation, this study provides a replicable framework for decarbonizing religious buildings in arid climates, contributing to UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 7 (Affordable Energy) and 11 (Sustainable Cities).
10.1109/TTE.2025.3581349: The electricity network (EN) and transportation network (TN) are becoming increasingly coupled and to ensure timely energy supply restoration of the coupling network after disasters; this study proposes an asynchronous decentralized load restoration method of the resilient electricity-transportation network (ETN) considering building and electric bus (E-Bus) coresponse. Initially, a coordinated restoration model of ETNs integrating building envelope thermal dynamic and E-Bus path planning models is proposed. Then, we leverage the natural cooling flexibility of the air conditioning (AC) and the spatial-temporal flexibility of the E-Bus to maximize the power supply time of loads and minimize the driving distance of E-Buses. Finally, to protect the information privacy between different subjects of the EN and TN, and reduce the computational burden, the double-judgment asynchronous decentralized alternating direction method of multipliers (DJAD-ADMMs) algorithm is proposed to solve the problem in a parallel manner. The results show that our method effectively enhances the restoration effect of critical loads by coordinating the potential flexibility of buildings and E-Buses while satisfying the temperature comfort demand of users and the terminal destination of E-Buses with enhanced solution efficiency.
10.1109/ICRERA66237.2025.11284095: Window solar heat gain significantly contributes to cooling energy demand in urban buildings, particularly during summer months and in dense cityscapes affected by the urban heat island effect. Vegetation has been shown to reduce this gain through shading, yet precise assessment of its impact at the sub-window level remains underexplored. This paper presents a high-resolution methodology for estimating the effect of vegetation on window solar heat gain using LiDAR-derived 3D environment comprising of 2.5 D grid, 3D building models and vegetation. Within this environment, solar heat gain is computed per window triangle by incorporating dynamic shading via ray-casting. Results demonstrate that vegetation reduces cumulative annual window solar heat gain by 11.31% in an urban setting, with greatest reductions observed on south-facing, upper-story windows and during summer months. The presented work provides detailed spatial insights into the thermal benefits of urban greenery and supports climate-sensitive urban planning and energy-efficient building design.
10.1109/SISIMPACT67725.2025.11439429: This study investigates the influence of different shading strategies—no shading, fixed shading, and louver shading—on solar heat gain through glass surfaces. Solar radiation, comprising direct and diffuse components, significantly contributes to indoor heat buildup and cooling loads in buildings. Without shading, daily heat gain values reach approximately 4.4-4.5 kWh, indicating maximum solar penetration. The application of fixed shading reduces this value to about 3.3 kWh, demonstrating its ability to block a portion of incident radiation, though with limited adaptability to variations in solar angle. In contrast, louver shading proves to be the most effective strategy, lowering daily heat gain to around 2.1-2.2 kWh. This reduction, nearly 50% compared to unshaded conditions, highlights the superior performance of louvers in minimizing direct and diffuse solar transmission while maintaining controlled daylight entry. Overall, the results emphasize that dynamic shading systems such as louvers are critical for improving energy efficiency, reducing cooling demand, and enhancing thermal comfort in sustainable building design.
10.1109/ELMA65795.2025.11083509: Agrivoltaic systems represent an emerging solution to the growing global need for sustainable energy and food production through the simultaneous use of land for agriculture and photovoltaic electricity generation. This paper presents the conceptual framework and justification for establishing a dedicated laboratory for agrivoltaic research. The proposed facility is designed to enable controlled experimentation, real-time monitoring, and optimization of key parameters such as energy efficiency, crop yield, microclimatic conditions, and system configurations. The laboratory integrates modern photovoltaic technologies, sensor networks, IoT platforms, and automated irrigation systems, creating a comprehensive environment for interdisciplinary research and education.
10.1109/SSDEE64538.2025.10967910: This paper demonstrates a brushless DC motor (BLDCM) fed water pumping system driven by the solar photovoltaic array (SPVA) under dynamic partial shading conditions. For extraction of maximum power from SPVA, a zeta converter (ZC) is utilized. However, under partial shading conditions, the SPVA experience multiple maximum power points (MPP). The conventional MPP tracking methods are ineffective in identifying the global MPP points as they converge to the local MPP points. Therefore, the utmost power cannot be extracted, when SPVA working under partially shaded conditions. Thus, this paper demonstrates the use of hybrid perturb & observe and particle swarm optimization techniques to track the global MPP. In this work, the SPVA's power extracted by ZC is fed to BLDCM for water pumping application using VSI. The VSI of a BLDCM typically functions at a significantly high frequency. This work proposes operating the VSI at a fundamental switching frequency to alleviate difficulties associated with high switching frequency. The suggested system is studied in MATLAB®/Simulink environment to validate its performance under various operational instances.
10.1109/SSI65953.2025.11107200: This study presents the development of an advanced façade system that integrates energy harvesting and Machine Learning (ML) to enhance thermal regulation and user comfort in residential buildings. The proposed system consists of automated outdoor blinds equipped with photovoltaic panels that dynamically adjust their orientation to maximize solar energy capture throughout the day. To further optimize indoor environmental conditions, low-cost screen-printed temperature, humidity, and carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors are embedded in the window frame, enabling real-time monitoring of ambient parameters. These sensor inputs support predictive control of window operation and climate regulation. Additionally, a mobile application allows users to monitor environmental conditions in real-time, manually control window settings, and receive energy efficiency recommendations. This research was conducted as part of the iPOWER project within the ILLIANCE consortium, which aims to develop innovative energy-saving solutions for sustainable building management
